output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ciarán Walsh has lived for eight years in a small stone house on the edge of Galway, where the salt wind has bleached the limewash to pale grey. He works remotely as a software engineer for a Dublin firm, known to colleagues only as an efficient voice on the line who never turns on his camera; when a build fails he says little, but within an hour he has pushed a cleanly documented fix. He is self-contained, methodical, and wary of attention. He grew up in a farming family inland from Galway and learned early that dependency meant vulnerability. His father was a quiet man who repaired his own machinery and said little at the dinner table. When Ciarán was fifteen, a summer storm collapsed a cattle shed, and the family spent a week salvaging timber and re-setting the roof without asking neighbours for help. That week hardened something in him; he discovered he could fix almost anything if he studied it carefully, and that he preferred to solve his own problems.

On weekends he sails his aging twenty-foot sloop, with a worn mainsail and a hull he patches himself. He knows every bolt, seam, and quirk of the engine, goes out alone for hours, never races, and avoids marina social gatherings. He returns at dusk, secures the lines, and walks home without a word. His neighbours expect only a raised hand or a brief nod. He does not attend local festivals, does not join the church committee, and does not stop for tea when a conversation lingers. Yet every Friday, without fail, he walks to the footbridge at the edge of the tidal marsh and replaces the broken step he noticed the week before. He carries a spare piece of treated oak in his rucksack, cuts it to size with a handsaw, and fits it while the morning mist is still low. No one sees him do it, but the step is always solid. He knows his neighbours use the bridge to reach the shops, and he knows they will never ask him for help. He prefers to give without being asked and to fix what is broken without explanation. His core tension is that he values independence above all, yet he cannot stand to see a small failure go unrepaired; he wants to be left alone, but he also wants to matter. The footbridge step is his compromise: a quiet proof of kindness so long as no one makes him speak it aloud.

His only sibling is his younger sister, Aoife, eight years his junior, who lives inland near Tuam. Their contact consists of a few short calls a year, mostly initiated by her. He helped her fit kitchen units two summers ago and left before tea was poured, as she expected. She knows he prefers solitude and never pushes, but she checks in when she is nearby. His established response tendencies include letting an unexpected family call ring and calling back later the same evening; when he does agree to meet someone, he arrives early and keeps the conversation brief. He has consistently declined casual neighbour invitations but has shown up for practical emergencies.

He values independence and self-reliance above all, a principle learned from a farming upbringing where dependency was seen as vulnerability and family problems were solved without outside help. He also values quiet, practical care for his community, expressed through the weekly footbridge repair. He has strong mechanical, electrical, and soldering skills, can fix almost anything by studying it carefully, is a knowledgeable sailor who maintains his own boat, and has professional software debugging and documentation abilities. He lives alone with a workbench in a back shed and has savings; his boat needs new rigging but he has no intention of buying it. He is settled with his solitude, though a stranger might notice how his eyes follow a child crossing the bridge or how he lingers when the harbour lights come on.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On Saturday afternoon, Ciarán is in the shed re-winding an alternator when his phone buzzes. It is his younger sister, Aoife, who rarely calls. She says she is driving back from a work trip, is passing through Galway, and is already at the petrol station near the footbridge. She has forty minutes before she needs to head inland to collect her children from school. She asks if he can meet her there for a coffee. He can see the station roof from his garden, but he is in the middle of a delicate solder job and has not showered since morning.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

He is kneeling on the shed floor, reheating a solder joint with steady, slightly tacky hands. He has not eaten since breakfast, his hair is flattened with sweat, and the alternator is half-wound. He had planned to finish this winding and then walk to the footbridge to re-check the step he replaced last Friday. The familiar ring of Aoife's number brings back the memory of her last call, which was to tell him about the children's school play. Looking toward the station roof, he remembers the Tuesday he saw her car parked there and assumed she was just filling up, only to learn later that she had waited an hour hoping he would come out.
